stories.title_en: Blinding and Cutting Off Feet to Cripple Children

paragraphs.zh: 浙中有等棍，常於通衢僻路，專候人家子女十數歲者，或迷路失歸，必拐帶去。擇其女有姿色，又絕聰明者，賣落院為娼。稍愚鈍者，刺瞎其雙眼，教之唱叫路歌曲；又或刖去足掌，致其拐腳。其刖足之法，每於隆冬極寒時，以麻扎幼童足肚，置腳掌於冷水中。浸得良久，以柴木指之曰：「痛否？」童應曰：「痛。」則又浸，及至冷極血凝，指亦不知痛，則以利刃刖斷其足掌，然後用藥敷之。後驅此雙瞽者、拐腳者，叫乞於道，每日責其丐錢米。多者與之飽食，少者痛酷捶打，令乞者方肯哀丐。晚复聚宿舟中。棍得其錢米，置美衣美食，在舟中歌唱為樂。暇或登岸，又四出拐帶，極為民害，而人不知。
paragraphs.en: In Zhejiang there are swindlers who wait on highways and lonely roads for other people’s children of ten-odd years. If a child loses the way home, they abduct him or her. They pick girls who are pretty and very clever, and sell them into brothels. The somewhat dull ones they blind in both eyes and teach to sing road-calling songs; or they cut off the soles of the feet, making them lame. The method of cutting feet: in the depths of winter, in extreme cold, they bind the child’s calves with hemp and put the soles in cold water. After soaking a long time, they point with a stick: “Does it hurt?” The child answers: “It hurts.” Then they soak more, until the cold is extreme, the blood frozen, and pointing no longer hurts; then they cut off the soles with a sharp blade, and apply medicine. Later they drive these double-blind and lame ones to beg on the roads, each day demanding they beg money and rice. Those who get much are given a full meal; those who get little are cruelly beaten, so the beggars will wail and beg. At night they gather to sleep on a boat. The swindlers take the money and rice, put on fine clothes, eat well, and sing for pleasure on the boat. In spare time they go ashore and abduct more in all directions—a great harm to the people, and people do not know.

paragraphs.zh: 一日，有小丐婆唱叫於路。居旁一老婦曰：「此丐婆好似李意五之女，其聲音亦似，只目瞎耳。」丐婆曰：「吾父正是李意五，吾有哥名鴉兒。五年前我往外婆家，不識路，被人引去，刺瞎兩眼，每日遣出叫化。有錢米歸，則有食；丐得稀少，便痛打無食，極是苦楚無奈。你聲音似我鄰居王二姆一般，千萬叫我娘與哥來認我，超度我出此地獄，你陰功如天。」王二姆聽其敘來歷皆真，收留入家曰：「你母今年已死，你兄遷居上巷，即遣人去喚來。」彼此皆相認得，遂具狀告於縣，批與主簿審。差人船中提二棍到。棍即用銀賄主簿；又用銀二十兩買其兄李鴉兒曰：「你令妹是他人拐帶，我收與眾乞合夥，非我刺她眼。況今已雙瞽，亦無人娶，不如與丐子為伴，亦不虧她衣食。」兄與官都得銀了，拘審時哥不堅認，主簿仍斷與棍去。棍引到船，撐入湖心痛打，以儆他丐，使後不敢漏洩。李丐婆叫屈連天，淒楚不忍聞。
paragraphs.en: One day a little beggar-woman was singing on the road. An old woman nearby said: “This beggar-girl looks like Li Yiwu’s daughter; her voice is like hers too, only she’s blind.” The beggar-woman said: “My father is exactly Li Yiwu; I have a brother named Ya’er. Five years ago I went to grandmother’s, didn’t know the road, was led away, blinded in both eyes, and sent out every day to beg. If I bring back money and rice, I eat; if I beg little, I’m beaten and get no food—bitter beyond bearing. Your voice is like my neighbor Aunt Wang Er; please, please call my mother and brother to recognize me, deliver me from this hell; your hidden merit will be like Heaven.” Aunt Wang Er heard the account of her origins was all true, took her into the house, and said: “Your mother died this year; your brother moved to the upper lane; I’ll send someone to call him.” They recognized each other, filed a complaint at the county; it was assigned to the assistant magistrate. Runners brought two swindlers from the boat. The swindlers bribed the assistant magistrate with silver; they also used twenty taels to buy the brother Li Ya’er, saying: “Your sister was abducted by others; I took her in with other beggars—I didn’t blind her. Besides she’s now double-blind; no one will marry her; better she stay with beggars as a companion; she won’t lack clothes and food.” Brother and official both took silver; at the hearing the brother would not firmly identify; the assistant magistrate still awarded her to the swindlers. They led her to the boat, poled to the lake center, and beat her cruelly as a warning to other beggars not to leak later. Li the beggar-woman cried injustice to Heaven; the misery was unbearable to hear.

paragraphs.zh: 船到向鄉官後門，聞溪中叫死聲，甚可憐，遣二家人去牽其船來，問打何人。眾丐指曰：「打李丐婆。」鄉官問：「因何打？」丐婆不敢說，只苦情求救。鄉官令引丐婆異處，再問曰：「你因何被這等苦打？明說來，我便救你。」李丐婆一一敘其前由。向鄉官聞情淒愴，不勝發忿，即鎖住四棍，並引眾丐入見太府，代陳其冤苦。太府亦切恨之，將四棍各打三十，曰：「此罪雖凌遲碎剮未足懲其罪，可鎖於府前，令眾人共毆之，以洩其忿。」眾人知此棍情，都來手毆石打，四棍一時皮破血吐，立刻盡死。後瞽目、拐腳眾丐，各問其鄉貫，家有人者，令其收養；無親屬者，各送入養濟院。人盡感向鄉官之仁，能除此四孽棍。
paragraphs.en: The boat came behind retired official Xiang’s back gate. He heard death-cries from the creek, very pitiful, sent two servants to pull the boat over, and asked whom they were beating. The beggars pointed: “Beating Li the beggar-woman.” The official asked why. She dared not say, only bitterly begged to be saved. The official had her led aside and asked again: “Why were you beaten so? Speak clearly and I’ll save you.” Li told the whole former story. Official Xiang heard, was grief-stricken and furious, locked up the four swindlers, led all the beggars to see the prefect, and stated their wrongs. The prefect also hated them bitterly, had each of the four beaten thirty strokes, and said: “Even lingering death by slicing would not be enough for this crime; lock them before the prefecture and let the crowd beat them to vent their rage.” People who knew these swindlers’ deeds all came, beating with hands and stones; the four at once had skin broken, vomited blood, and died on the spot. Later the blind and lame beggars were each asked their native place; those with family were sent to be taken in; those without relatives were sent to poorhouses. Everyone was grateful for Official Xiang’s humanity, able to remove these four evil swindlers.

paragraphs.zh: 按：人家子女幼稚，不可令其單行，亦不可帶金銀鐲錢。若偶遇此等棍，悔何可及！其防於未失之先可也。今後官府遇瞎拐群集處時，遣人查其居止，及提問一二瘸瞎緣由，或訪得此等棍，則除一棍勝去一狼虎也，功德高於浮屠矣。
paragraphs.en: Note: People’s young children must not be allowed to go alone, nor wear gold and silver bangles. If they happen to meet such swindlers, regret comes too late! Guard before the loss. From now on, when officials meet clusters of blind and lame beggars, send people to check where they live, and question one or two about how they became lame or blind; if such swindlers are found, removing one swindler is better than removing a wolf or tiger; the merit is higher than a stupa.

stories.title_en: A Eunuch Cooks Boys and Eats Their Marrow

paragraphs.zh: 朝廷往往聽言利之臣，命太監四出抽分，名為徵商抑末以重農本，實則商稅重而轉賣之處必貴，則買之價增，而買者受其害；商不通而出物之處必賤，則賣之價減，而賣者受其害。利雖僅取及商，而四民皆陰耗其財，以供朝廷之暗取，尤甚於明加田稅也。且徵榷之利，朝廷得一，太監得十，稅官得百，巡卒得千，是民費千百金，以奉朝廷之一金，益上者少而損下者無涯矣。然巡卒、稅官之實溪壑，猶是普天率土之民得飽暖也。特不耕不織而魚肉下民，不免坐蠹天地間服食。若太監攘剝既多，崇聚盈溢，視錦繡如敝葉，視金玉如瓦礫。服食器用，皆與天子同；指使承順，如奉天子同。人間福分享受，無不窮極；獨恨不能淫樂女色，所少者此耳。嘗命左右，訪有復生陽物之方，購以萬金。
paragraphs.en: The court often listens to ministers who talk of profit, and orders eunuchs out in all directions to levy extra duties, called “taxing merchants and suppressing the secondary occupations to weight agriculture.” In fact, when commercial taxes are heavy, resale places get expensive, buying prices rise, and buyers suffer; trade does not flow, producing places get cheap, selling prices fall, and sellers suffer. Though the profit is taken only from merchants, all four classes of people secretly lose wealth to supply the court’s hidden taking, worse than openly raising the land tax. And of the levy’s profit, the court gets one, the eunuch ten, tax officials a hundred, patrol runners a thousand: so the people spend a thousand or a hundred taels to present the court one tael; what benefits above is little, what harms below is boundless. Yet filling the gullies of runners and tax officials still means people under Heaven get food and warmth. Only those who neither plow nor weave, who prey on the common people, inevitably sit as worms among Heaven and Earth’s food and clothing. As for eunuchs, having seized and stripped so much, piled up to overflowing, they see brocade as worn leaves, gold and jade as tiles. Clothes, food, and utensils all match the Son of Heaven; those they order about serve them as they would the Son of Heaven. Human good fortune they enjoy to the extreme; they only resent they cannot have pleasure with women—that is all they lack. They often ordered attendants to seek a method to restore the male organ, offering ten thousand taels.

paragraphs.zh: 有方外道士，利得其金也，私臆懸度，謂「古方云『土以土補，木以木補，人以人補』，意必食人可補人也。」妄去獻方云：「烹童男膾肝脯肉，食其精髓，則精液充滿，陽物復生，可姦婦生子矣。」閩高閹信之，先售以百金，候服有驗，再來領萬金。由是，命牙爪往窮鄉僻邑，買貧民幼童，詐云「高衙欲養為子，日後富貴無窮。」貧民信之，多賣以博眼前重利，且希望後日富貴。後先買者，難以稽數。但鬻子之家，有託人往​​查己子者，並無聲息；即衙中走僕，亦不知內之養子若何也。原來買之幼童，盡養以錦衣美食。廚子能烹調一童以進食，賞銀十兩，深禁其秘密。每殺一童，廚子提刀追趕，眾童各涕泣奔呼，候其走熱氣揚，則執其肥者烹之。
paragraphs.en: A wandering Daoist, greedy for the gold, privately guessed: “The old formula says ‘earth supplements earth, wood supplements wood, man supplements man’—so eating people should supplement a man.” He rashly offered a formula: “Boil a boy, slice the liver, dry the flesh, eat the essence and marrow, then the seminal fluid will fill, the organ will grow back, and you can have women and sons.” Eunuch Gao of Fujian believed it, first paid a hundred taels, to wait and see if taking it worked, then come for the ten thousand. Thus he ordered his claws and teeth to poor villages and remote counties, buying poor people’s young boys, lying: “Gao’s yamen wants to raise them as sons; later wealth and honor without end.” The poor believed; many sold for heavy present profit, and hoping for later honor. Those bought first and after are hard to count. But among families who sold sons, some asked people to go inquire after their own sons—no news at all; even servants walking in the yamen did not know how the adopted sons inside were. Originally the bought boys were all raised in silk clothes and fine food. A cook who could stew one boy and present it was rewarded ten taels; they were strictly forbidden to speak. Each time a boy was killed, the cook chased with a knife; the boys wept and ran crying; when they had run hot and their qi was up, he seized the fat ones and cooked them.

paragraphs.zh: 內有一童十二歲，跪廚子涕泣哀告，叩頭求救。廚子亦淚曰：「吾怎能救你，吾亦不奈何墮此也。」有頃，外人傳某鄉官相拜。廚子曰：「憑你命，吾放你出去，外有鄉官相拜，你扯其衣死哀求救；肯帶你去，則你可生，我代你死罷。你可傳知外人，切勿將子賣入太監府也。」此幼童直奔至鄉官前，哀告：「廚子要殺我！」太監即令查拿廚子斬首，———彼恨其縱出此童也，笑顏諭幼童入後。幼童死扯鄉官衣求救。鄉官疑有緣故，為之帶出。幼童歷敘內中殺諸童之由，鄉官不勝嗟嘆。思起本未得諸童買來之由，又無廚子證據，亦不敢留養此童，遣其出外別投生。此童後流丐於建郡等處。人問其太監府之事，多能言其中之富貴，皆非人世所有也。自後方知太監之食人，始不肯以子賣之。近年，高閹以罪去。其鬻子之父母，累十百候於途，並不見一幼子與姦閹生去者，無不墮淚，痛其子之必遭烹也。
paragraphs.en: Among them a twelve-year-old knelt to the cook, weeping, kowtowing for his life. The cook also wept: “How can I save you? I too had no choice but to fall into this.” Shortly, word from outside: a certain retired official had come to pay respects. The cook said: “As your fate has it, I’ll let you out; outside a retired official is calling; grab his clothes and wail for your life; if he’ll take you, you may live, and I’ll die in your place. Tell people outside: never sell a son into a eunuch’s residence.” The boy ran straight to the official and cried: “The cook wants to kill me!” The eunuch immediately ordered the cook seized and beheaded—he hated him for letting the boy out—then with a smile told the boy to go in back. The boy clung dead to the official’s clothes begging to be saved. The official suspected a reason and took him out. The boy told in full why the boys inside were being killed; the official sighed without end. Thinking he had never gotten the origin of how the boys were bought, and without the cook as witness, he dared not keep and raise this boy, and sent him out to seek another living. The boy later drifted begging around Jian prefecture and such places. When people asked about the eunuch’s residence, he could often tell of riches inside that were not of this world. Only then did people know eunuchs ate people, and began to refuse to sell sons to them. In recent years Eunuch Gao was removed for crimes. Parents who had sold sons, tens and hundreds, waited on the road, and not one young son was seen going off with the wicked eunuch; none failed to shed tears, grieving that their sons must have been cooked.

paragraphs.zh: 按：貧民賣子，極為至愚。若不能養，何不若鳳陽府父子俱丐，猶可骨肉相保。必不得已，唯可賣之富戶為僕。固不可供太監之啖，亦不可賣入庵寺為行童侍者，其賤尤在乞丐下也。國家置閹尹，以供掃除傳命耳。至使握利權，享用已極，更思生陽物淫婦人，為不可必得之事。雖食人而可為汝欲扶已朽之軀，曾不惜人渾全之命乎？是可忍也，孰不可忍也！孟子曰：「善戰者服上刑」，猶為強兵而殺人也；此為何事而視人命如草菅乎？王法若明，當不令此閹得生還矣。
paragraphs.en: Note: Poor people selling sons is the height of folly. If you cannot raise them, why not, like Fengyang prefecture, father and son both beg, still keeping flesh and bone together? If you must, you may only sell them to a rich house as servants. You must not supply a eunuch’s eating, nor sell them into convents and temples as novices and attendants—that is even lower than beggars. The state sets eunuchs to sweep and pass orders. To let them grasp the profit-power, enjoy to the extreme, then think of growing an organ to debauch women—a thing they cannot possibly get. Even if eating people could prop up your already rotten body for your desire, would you not spare a person’s whole life? If this can be borne, what cannot be borne! Mencius said “those good at war should suffer the heaviest punishment”—still, that is killing people for a strong army; for what business is this, treating human life as grass? If the king’s law were clear, this eunuch should not have been allowed to return alive.
